title: The Compromise at the Heart of Translation
text:
Literary translation is often described as an act of interpretation rather than mere substitution. A translator must decide whether to preserve the rhythm of a sentence, its ambiguities, or its cultural references, knowing that no single choice can satisfy every dimension at once. Consider a line of poetry whose charm lies in a pun: the translator may abandon the wordplay entirely, or may invent a new pun that serves the same comic function. Each option sacrifices something, and the result is always a negotiation rather than a faithful copy.

Critics have long debated whether a translation should read as if it were originally written in the target language or should retain the flavour of its source. Those who favour the first approach argue that a text which feels foreign on every page will fail to engage ordinary readers. Those who favour the second contend that smoothing away the strangeness of the original erases the very experience the author intended to convey. Most accomplished translators, in practice, adopt a position somewhere between these extremes.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what must a translator decide?
options: Whether to preserve rhythm, ambiguity, or cultural references
Whether to publish the translation in two languages
Whether the original author should approve the work
Whether to shorten the poem to a single line

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do critics debate?
options: Whether translators should be paid by the page
Whether a translation should read as if originally written in the target language or keep its source flavour
Whether poetry can be translated at all
Whether readers prefer modern or old-fashioned words

questions.text: What can be inferred from the example of the pun?
options: Wordplay always translates without any loss
Translators should ignore humour in literature
Some meaning must be sacrificed or reinvented when a pun is translated
Puns are rarely found in poetry

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about most accomplished translators?
options: They strictly follow one of the two extreme approaches
They avoid making decisions about style
They generally combine elements of both approaches rather than picking one extreme
They prefer to work without reading critics

paragraph_translations: Literary translation is often described as explaining meaning rather than simply swapping words. A translator has to choose whether to keep a sentence's rhythm, its uncertain meanings, or its cultural references, and no single choice can satisfy all of them at once. Take a line of poetry whose appeal depends on a pun: the translator may drop the wordplay completely, or may create a new pun that does the same comic job. Every option gives something up, so the result is always a compromise rather than an exact copy.

Critics have long argued over whether a translation should sound as though it was originally written in the target language, or should keep the character of its source. People who prefer the first approach say that a text which feels foreign on every page will not hold ordinary readers. People who prefer the second say that smoothing out the original's strangeness removes the very experience the author wanted to share. In practice, most skilled translators take a middle position between these extremes.
